title: Top 5 most streamed songs in 2023
task: Return the top 5 tracks in the entire 2023 dataset snapshot, by known streams. This does not measure streams earned during 2023. Return track_name, artist_name, released_year, streams. Break ties by track_name then artist_name.
note: A top-N sort avoids fully ordering all rows. Exclude unknown streams explicitly. A release-year filter would answer a different question.
steps: Start with the full snapshot: do not filter released_year when the question asks for the most streamed tracks in this dataset.
Remove unknown stream totals, sort the remaining totals descending, and use title and artist as tie-breakers.
LIMIT 5 keeps the first five rows after ordering.

title: Unique contributing artists
task: Estimate distinct individual artist names by splitting artist_name on commas and trimming spaces; remove empty tokens. Output unique_artists. This assumes commas separate credits; names containing commas and spelling/encoding variants make this an estimate.
sql:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT a.artist) AS unique_artists FROM public.spotify s
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT DISTINCT btrim(v) AS artist FROM unnest(string_to_array(s.artist_name, ',')) AS u(v) WHERE btrim(v) <> '') a;
note: COUNT(DISTINCT artist_name) counts credit combinations, not individual artists. Splitting expands rows; at larger scale use artist and track_artist tables with stable IDs.
steps: Split each artist credit string on commas, then trim whitespace from each token.
The lateral subquery expands each track into its credited names and discards empty names.
COUNT(DISTINCT artist) counts parsed names, not credit combinations. This is still an estimate of real identities.

title: Songs across release years
task: Return released_year, songs, pct_of_dataset (2 decimals), ascending year.
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: GROUP BY released_year creates one group per release year.
COUNT(*) counts stored observations in each year.
SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () totals the grouped counts; multiply by 100.0 to avoid integer division, then round.

title: Top 10 artists and their audio features
task: Popularity proxy = total known streams, with full track credit to each parsed individual artist. Output artist, tracks, known_stream_tracks, total_streams, avg_danceability, avg_energy (averages 2 decimals). Rank descending total_streams NULLS LAST then artist; limit 10. Full credit means totals are not additive across artists.
sql:
SELECT a.artist, COUNT(*) AS tracks, COUNT(streams) AS known_stream_tracks,
SUM(streams) AS total_streams, ROUND(AVG(danceability_pct),2) AS avg_danceability, ROUND(AVG(energy_pct),2) AS avg_energy
FROM public.spotify s CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT DISTINCT btrim(v) AS artist FROM unnest(string_to_array(s.artist_name, ',')) AS u(v) WHERE btrim(v) <> '') a
GROUP BY a.artist ORDER BY total_streams DESC NULLS LAST, a.artist LIMIT 10;
note: Split credits once, then group. Deduplicate repeated tokens within a track. AVG of features includes all that artist’s tracks, even one with unknown streams.
steps: Expand each track into distinct parsed artist credits. Give every credited artist full credit for the track.
Group by individual artist and compute track count, known stream count, summed streams and average audio features.
Order total streams descending with unknown totals last and keep ten artists. Audio averages include tracks even when their streams are unknown.

title: Artists with longest and shortest songs
task: Schema reasoning: determine whether this is answerable. Query metadata for duration columns, returning column_name and data_type. Explain the missing information rather than substituting BPM or title length.
note: Not answerable: no duration column. Empty metadata output is the expected result. Obtain duration_ms plus reliable track IDs before answering.
steps: Inspect information_schema.columns rather than guessing a duration field.
Filter the actual table metadata for column names containing duration.
The empty result shows that this schema cannot answer longest or shortest songs; request duration and reliable track IDs.

title: Most Spotify playlists
task: Return every track tied for maximum in_spotify_playlists: track_name, artist_name, in_spotify_playlists. Order by track_name, artist_name.
note: Two small scans are fine; MAX preserves all ties, unlike LIMIT 1.
steps: Calculate the highest Spotify playlist count with MAX.
Keep every row equal to that maximum, preserving ties.
Order the tied rows by title and artist for a stable displayed result.

title: Streams vs Spotify charts
task: Correlate streams with the number of Spotify charts containing the track. Chart counts are not chart ranks. Output paired_tracks and pearson_r rounded to 4 decimals; use only rows where both values are known.
sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS paired_tracks, ROUND(CORR(streams, in_spotify_charts)::numeric,4) AS pearson_r
FROM public.spotify WHERE streams IS NOT NULL AND in_spotify_charts IS NOT NULL;
note: CORR computes Pearson correlation in one scan. It measures linear association, not causation; inspect outliers and skew before interpreting it. NULL correlation means insufficient pairs or zero variance.
steps: Use only tracks where streams and Spotify chart count are both known.
CORR calculates Pearson linear correlation across those pairs.
Return the paired sample count alongside the rounded coefficient; chart counts are not chart positions.

title: Average BPM
task: Output tracks_with_bpm and avg_bpm rounded to 2 decimals, across the entire table.
sql: SELECT COUNT(bpm) AS tracks_with_bpm, ROUND(AVG(bpm),2) AS avg_bpm FROM public.spotify;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: AVG(bpm) averages known BPM values; COUNT(bpm) reports how many values contribute.
Round only the displayed average to two decimal places.

title: Danceability of top 15 tracks
task: Popularity proxy = known streams. Take exactly 15 tracks ordered by streams DESC, track_name, artist_name. Output tracks and avg_danceability rounded to 2 decimals.
note: Apply LIMIT before AVG. Averaging all rows then adding LIMIT does not answer this question.
steps: The inner query first selects exactly 15 tracks by known streams, using the declared tie-breakers.
The outer query averages danceability only within that selected set.
Putting LIMIT after an aggregate over the whole table would not select the top tracks first.

title: Both Apple Music and Spotify charts
task: Presence means a chart count greater than zero. Output songs.
sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS songs FROM public.spotify WHERE in_apple_charts > 0 AND in_spotify_charts > 0;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: A positive count indicates chart presence.
Use AND so a track must meet both platform conditions, then count qualifying rows.

title: Apple playlist presence and valence
task: Compare absent (0), present (>0), and unknown (NULL) groups, returning playlist_presence, tracks, avg_valence (2 decimals), sorted by playlist_presence. Only observed groups need appear.
note: An average difference is descriptive; it does not establish statistical significance or an effect caused by playlists.
steps: Use CASE to distinguish positive playlist counts, zero counts and unknown counts.
Group by that classification and compute sample size and average valence.
Compare the groups descriptively; playlist presence does not prove a cause of valence.

title: Deezer charts by release month
task: Use release months across all years, not historical chart movements. Output released_month, tracks, charted_tracks (>0), charted_pct (2 decimals of known counts), avg_chart_count (2 decimals). Sort by month.
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Group all tracks by release month across the dataset’s release years.
Use a FILTER to count confirmed Deezer chart appearances.
Divide by known chart counts for the appearance rate, and retain the average chart count and group size.

title: Both Deezer and Spotify playlists
task: Count tracks with both playlist counts greater than zero. Output songs.
sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS songs FROM public.spotify WHERE in_deezer_playlists > 0 AND in_spotify_playlists > 0;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Require positive counts for both Deezer playlists and Spotify playlists.
COUNT(*) returns the number of track observations meeting both conditions.

title: Shazam performance and danceability
task: Define high presence as >=100 Shazam charts; low presence as 1–99; absent as 0; unknown as NULL. Return shazam_group, tracks, avg_danceability (2 decimals), alphabetical group order. The 100 threshold is an exercise convention, not a validated success criterion.
sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN in_shazam_charts IS NULL THEN 'unknown' WHEN in_shazam_charts >=100 THEN 'high' WHEN in_shazam_charts>0 THEN 'low' ELSE 'absent' END AS shazam_group,
COUNT(*) AS tracks, ROUND(AVG(danceability_pct),2) AS avg_danceability FROM public.spotify GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Use CASE to create the declared Shazam groups: unknown, high (100+), low (1–99), and absent.
Aggregate track counts and mean danceability per group.
The threshold is a convention for this exercise; it is not a universal definition of success.

title: Speechiness distribution on Shazam
task: For tracks on >0 Shazam charts, bucket speechiness into 0–9, 10–19, …, 90–100. Output bucket_start, tracks and pct (2 decimals). Only occupied bins; sort by bucket_start.
sql:
WITH b AS (SELECT LEAST(speechiness_pct / 10,9)*10 AS bucket_start FROM public.spotify
WHERE in_shazam_charts>0 AND speechiness_pct IS NOT NULL)
SELECT bucket_start, COUNT(*) AS tracks, ROUND(100.0*COUNT(*)/SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (),2) AS pct
FROM b GROUP BY bucket_start ORDER BY bucket_start;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Keep tracks appearing on at least one Shazam chart and with known speechiness.
Integer division creates decade bins; LEAST places a value of 100 into the final 90–100 bin.
Count occupied bins and divide by the total eligible count to get percentages.

title: Major vs minor danceability
task: Output mode, tracks, avg_danceability (2 decimals), ordered by mode. Describe the difference without claiming significance.
sql: SELECT mode, COUNT(*) AS tracks, ROUND(AVG(danceability_pct),2) AS avg_danceability FROM public.spotify GROUP BY mode ORDER BY mode;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Group observations by mode.
Compute each group’s count and average danceability; order by mode.
Describe the difference without claiming it is statistically significant.

title: Acousticness distribution by key
task: Output key (keep NULL as unknown), tracks, min_acousticness, p25, median, p75, max_acousticness, avg_acousticness. Round percentiles and average to 2 decimals; order by key NULLS LAST.
sql:
SELECT key, COUNT(*) AS tracks, MIN(acousticness_pct) AS min_acousticness,
ROUND((PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY acousticness_pct))::numeric,2) AS p25,
ROUND((PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY acousticness_pct))::numeric,2) AS median,
ROUND((PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY acousticness_pct))::numeric,2) AS p75,
MAX(acousticness_pct) AS max_acousticness, ROUND(AVG(acousticness_pct),2) AS avg_acousticness
FROM public.spotify GROUP BY key ORDER BY key NULLS LAST;
note: Ordered-set percentiles require sorting values. Keep group counts visible; small samples make comparisons unstable.
steps: Group by key, keeping NULL as a separate unknown group.
Calculate minimum, maximum, average, and continuous quartiles of acousticness within each group.
Percentiles describe the distribution rather than only its center; compare group sizes too.

title: Energy by release year
task: Output released_year, tracks, avg_energy (2 decimals), ordered by year. These are release cohorts in this sample, not the whole music industry over time.
sql: SELECT released_year, COUNT(*) AS tracks, ROUND(AVG(energy_pct),2) AS avg_energy FROM public.spotify GROUP BY released_year ORDER BY released_year;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Group tracks by release year and calculate average energy.
Keep the number of observations visible so sparse years are recognizable.
These are release cohorts in a selected snapshot, not historical measurements of all music.

title: Most common keys
task: Return key, tracks, pct_of_dataset (2 decimals); include NULL separately. Sort tracks descending then key NULLS LAST.
sql:
SELECT key, COUNT(*) AS tracks, ROUND(100.0*COUNT(*)/SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (),2) AS pct_of_dataset
FROM public.spotify GROUP BY key ORDER BY tracks DESC, key NULLS LAST;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Group by musical key, including unknown keys as a separate group.
Count each group and divide by the whole dataset count for its share.
Sort counts descending to identify the most represented keys.

title: Artist count for charted songs
task: Charted = >0 on at least one of Spotify, Apple, Deezer or Shazam charts. Output charted_tracks and avg_artist_count (2 decimals). An unknown count alone does not prove presence.
sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS charted_tracks, ROUND(AVG(artist_count),2) AS avg_artist_count FROM public.spotify WHERE (in_spotify_charts > 0 OR in_apple_charts > 0 OR in_deezer_charts > 0 OR in_shazam_charts > 0);
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Combine the four chart-presence tests with OR: any confirmed appearance qualifies.
Count qualifying tracks and average their recorded artist_count.
NULL on one platform does not block a confirmed positive count on another.

title: Artist count vs danceability
task: Group by artist_count; output artist_count, tracks, avg_danceability (2 decimals), ordered by artist_count. Compare observed groups without asserting causation.
sql: SELECT artist_count, COUNT(*) AS tracks, ROUND(AVG(danceability_pct),2) AS avg_danceability FROM public.spotify GROUP BY artist_count ORDER BY artist_count;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Group by the recorded artist_count instead of splitting artist names.
Compute sample sizes and average danceability for each collaboration size.
Compare the averages and their group sizes; this alone cannot show causation.

title: Valence by release month in 2023
task: Restrict released_year=2023. Output released_month, tracks, avg_valence, p25, median, p75 (2 decimals), ordered by month. Only observed months; missing months do not mean zero releases.
sql:
SELECT released_month, COUNT(*) AS tracks, ROUND(AVG(valence_pct),2) AS avg_valence,
ROUND((PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY valence_pct))::numeric,2) AS p25,
ROUND((PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY valence_pct))::numeric,2) AS median,
ROUND((PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY valence_pct))::numeric,2) AS p75
FROM public.spotify WHERE released_year=2023 GROUP BY released_month ORDER BY released_month;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Filter to tracks released in 2023 before grouping by release month.
Calculate average valence and quartiles to show the distribution within each observed month.
Do not invent zeros for months missing from this sample.

title: Key patterns across years
task: Return released_year, key, tracks, pct_within_year (2 decimals). Include unknown keys; order year then key NULLS LAST. Interpret as this snapshot’s release cohorts.
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Group by both release year and key.
A window partitioned by release year totals the key counts for each year.
Divide each key’s count by its own year total, keeping unknown keys in that denominator.

title: Cross-platform presence
task: Operational definition: a positive chart count on all four platforms. Return track_name, artist_name, streams and all four chart counts. Order known streams descending NULLS LAST then track_name, artist_name. This replaces the undefined word significant; no statistical significance is claimed.
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Use AND across all four positive chart-count conditions.
Return the individual platform counts so the cross-platform presence can be inspected.
Sort by known stream totals descending and keep unknown stream totals last.

title: Stream distribution vs Apple charts
task: Group Apple chart counts as absent (0), present (>0), unknown (NULL). Output apple_chart_presence, tracks, known_stream_tracks, min_streams, avg_streams, median_streams, max_streams. Round average/median to 2 decimals; sort by group.
sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN in_apple_charts IS NULL THEN 'unknown' WHEN in_apple_charts>0 THEN 'present' ELSE 'absent' END AS apple_chart_presence,
COUNT(*) AS tracks, COUNT(streams) AS known_stream_tracks, MIN(streams) AS min_streams, ROUND(AVG(streams),2) AS avg_streams,
ROUND((PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY streams))::numeric,2) AS median_streams, MAX(streams) AS max_streams
FROM public.spotify GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Classify Apple chart presence into positive, zero or unknown.
For each group, report total tracks and known stream totals separately.
Compare minimum, median, mean and maximum streams; skew can make the mean differ greatly from the median.

title: BPM vs danceability
task: Measure linear association. Output paired_tracks and pearson_r rounded to 4 decimals; use only rows where both values are known.
sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS paired_tracks, ROUND(CORR(bpm, danceability_pct)::numeric,4) AS pearson_r
FROM public.spotify WHERE bpm IS NOT NULL AND danceability_pct IS NOT NULL;
note: CORR computes Pearson correlation in one scan. It measures linear association, not causation; inspect outliers and skew before interpreting it. NULL correlation means insufficient pairs or zero variance.
steps: Select pairs with known BPM and danceability.
CORR measures their linear association and COUNT reports its sample size.
Round the output coefficient; do not confuse association with a causal effect.

title: Liveness vs acousticness
task: Measure linear association. Liveness is an audio feature, not verified concert attendance. Output paired_tracks and pearson_r rounded to 4 decimals; use only rows where both values are known.
sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS paired_tracks, ROUND(CORR(liveness_pct, acousticness_pct)::numeric,4) AS pearson_r
FROM public.spotify WHERE liveness_pct IS NOT NULL AND acousticness_pct IS NOT NULL;
note: CORR computes Pearson correlation in one scan. It measures linear association, not causation; inspect outliers and skew before interpreting it. NULL correlation means insufficient pairs or zero variance.
steps: Select known liveness and acousticness pairs.
Compute Pearson correlation and report the number of pairs.
Liveness is an audio feature estimate, not proof that a song was recorded at a concert.

title: Valence vs streams
task: Measure linear association of valence and known stream totals. Output paired_tracks and pearson_r rounded to 4 decimals; use only rows where both values are known.
sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS paired_tracks, ROUND(CORR(valence_pct, streams)::numeric,4) AS pearson_r
FROM public.spotify WHERE valence_pct IS NOT NULL AND streams IS NOT NULL;
note: CORR computes Pearson correlation in one scan. It measures linear association, not causation; inspect outliers and skew before interpreting it. NULL correlation means insufficient pairs or zero variance.
steps: Exclude unknown valence or stream values from the paired sample.
Compute Pearson correlation on the raw values.
Streams can be strongly skewed; a single coefficient can hide outliers or nonlinear relationships.

title: Spotify playlists vs Apple charts
task: Measure linear association between the two counts. Output paired_tracks and pearson_r rounded to 4 decimals; use only rows where both values are known.
sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS paired_tracks, ROUND(CORR(in_spotify_playlists, in_apple_charts)::numeric,4) AS pearson_r
FROM public.spotify WHERE in_spotify_playlists IS NOT NULL AND in_apple_charts IS NOT NULL;
note: CORR computes Pearson correlation in one scan. It measures linear association, not causation; inspect outliers and skew before interpreting it. NULL correlation means insufficient pairs or zero variance.
steps: Pair Spotify playlist counts with Apple chart counts for each track.
Compute the correlation and paired sample count.
The two metrics measure different kinds of presence; correlation does not imply one causes the other.

title: Key and mode combinations
task: Output key, mode, tracks, pct_of_dataset (2 decimals). Include unknown keys; order tracks DESC, key NULLS LAST, mode.
sql:
SELECT key, mode, COUNT(*) AS tracks, ROUND(100.0*COUNT(*)/SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (),2) AS pct_of_dataset
FROM public.spotify GROUP BY key,mode ORDER BY tracks DESC,key NULLS LAST,mode;
note: Use one aggregation pass where possible; only sort the final grouped result.
steps: Group by both key and mode to count every observed combination.
Use the total of grouped counts for whole-dataset percentages.
Sort by descending count and then the requested tie-breakers; keep unknown key groups.

title: Speechiness in different Apple playlists
task: Original question cannot identify individual playlists: only their counts exist. Adaptation: compare count bands 0, 1–49, 50–99, 100+, unknown. Output playlist_band, tracks, avg_speechiness (2 decimals), alphabetical band order.
sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN in_apple_playlists IS NULL THEN 'unknown' WHEN in_apple_playlists=0 THEN '0' WHEN in_apple_playlists<50 THEN '1-49' WHEN in_apple_playlists<100 THEN '50-99' ELSE '100+' END AS playlist_band,
COUNT(*) AS tracks, ROUND(AVG(speechiness_pct),2) AS avg_speechiness FROM public.spotify GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
note: This answers an explicitly adapted question. Actual playlist comparisons require playlist IDs and a track-to-playlist membership table.
steps: Recognize that playlist identities are unavailable: this adaptation groups by playlist-count bands.
CASE assigns each row to the specified band.
Compute mean speechiness and sample size for each band, without claiming these are individual playlist comparisons.

title: Release-day patterns and charts
task: Interpret release day as day of week. Derive dates from year, month, day. Output iso_weekday (Monday=1), tracks, charted_tracks (any of four platforms >0), charted_pct (2 decimals, denominator all tracks in weekday group). Sort weekday. Missing chart counts do not confirm absence; percentage is confirmed-presence rate.
note: Use MAKE_DATE only after validating component dates. A high charted count may simply reflect more releases on that weekday; compare rates and sample sizes.
steps: MAKE_DATE builds a date from the validated release components.
EXTRACT(ISODOW) derives Monday=1 through Sunday=7, and OR defines confirmed appearance on any chart.
Group by weekday and compare both confirmed counts and their share of all tracks in that weekday group.

title: Instrumentalness vs energy
task: Measure linear association. Output paired_tracks and pearson_r rounded to 4 decimals; use only rows where both values are known.
sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS paired_tracks, ROUND(CORR(instrumentalness_pct, energy_pct)::numeric,4) AS pearson_r
FROM public.spotify WHERE instrumentalness_pct IS NOT NULL AND energy_pct IS NOT NULL;
note: CORR computes Pearson correlation in one scan. It measures linear association, not causation; inspect outliers and skew before interpreting it. NULL correlation means insufficient pairs or zero variance.
steps: Use known instrumentalness and energy pairs.
Return the paired count and Pearson linear correlation.
Interpret this feature association without claiming a mechanism or cause.

title: Outliers and anomalies
task: Return a diagnostic table: check_name, affected_rows. Checks: missing streams/key/Shazam; duplicate extra rows by track_name+artist_name+release date; invalid percentage feature rows; nonpositive BPM; comma-token count mismatch vs artist_count; streams above Q3+1.5*IQR. Sort by check_name. Outliers are flags, not automatic errors.
sql:
WITH quartiles AS (SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY streams) AS q1, PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY streams) AS q3 FROM public.spotify),
duplicates AS (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM public.spotify GROUP BY track_name, artist_name, released_year, released_month, released_day HAVING COUNT(*)>1),
checks AS (
SELECT 'missing_streams' AS check_name, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE streams IS NULL) AS affected_rows FROM public.spotify
UNION ALL SELECT 'missing_key', COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE key IS NULL) FROM public.spotify
UNION ALL SELECT 'missing_shazam', COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE in_shazam_charts IS NULL) FROM public.spotify
UNION ALL SELECT 'duplicate_extra_rows', COALESCE(SUM(n-1),0)::bigint FROM duplicates
UNION ALL SELECT 'invalid_percentage_rows', COUNT(*) FROM public.spotify s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM unnest(ARRAY[danceability_pct,valence_pct,energy_pct,acousticness_pct,instrumentalness_pct,liveness_pct,speechiness_pct]) v WHERE v<0 OR v>100)
UNION ALL SELECT 'nonpositive_bpm', COUNT(*) FROM public.spotify WHERE bpm<=0
UNION ALL SELECT 'artist_token_count_mismatch', COUNT(*) FROM public.spotify WHERE cardinality(string_to_array(artist_name,','))<>artist_count
UNION ALL SELECT 'high_streams_iqr_outlier', COUNT(*) FROM public.spotify CROSS JOIN quartiles WHERE streams>q3+1.5*(q3-q1)
) SELECT * FROM checks ORDER BY check_name;
note: The diagnostic is intentionally readable, with several scans. For large data combine simple checks using FILTER in one scan. Duplicate candidates lack track IDs; do not delete them automatically. This does not exhaust every possible anomaly.
steps: Compute stream quartiles and flag values above Q3 plus 1.5 times the interquartile range.
Separately count missing fields, candidate duplicate extra rows, invalid percentages, nonpositive BPM and artist-credit mismatches.
Combine named checks with UNION ALL. Flags identify observations to investigate; they do not justify deleting data.

title: Popularity rankings for each key
task: Create a result table (SELECT, not a persistent table). Popularity proxy = average known streams per key. Exclude unknown keys. Output popularity_rank (DENSE_RANK), key, tracks, known_stream_tracks, avg_streams (2 decimals), total_streams. Rank on unrounded averages descending NULLS LAST; order rank then key.
note: Group before window ranking; the window only sorts a handful of keys. Average and total streams answer different definitions of popularity.
steps: Group known keys and compute average known streams, total streams and track counts.
Apply DENSE_RANK to unrounded averages: equal averages share a rank with no rank gaps.
Round only the displayed mean and order by rank then key. This is a result table, not CREATE TABLE.

title: Key popularity vs representation in top 50
task: Top 50 = entire snapshot, not only songs released in 2023; exclude unknown streams. Tie-break by track_name then artist_name. Exclude unknown keys from key rankings but keep them eligible for the top 50. Output popularity_rank, key, avg_streams (2 decimals), top50_tracks, top50_pct (of all 50; 2 decimals), representation_rank (DENSE_RANK by count). Include known keys with zero top-50 tracks; order popularity_rank,key.
sql:
WITH k AS (SELECT key, AVG(streams) AS mean_streams FROM public.spotify WHERE key IS NOT NULL GROUP BY key),
top50 AS (SELECT key FROM public.spotify WHERE streams IS NOT NULL ORDER BY streams DESC,track_name,artist_name LIMIT 50),
c AS (SELECT key,COUNT(*) AS n FROM top50 GROUP BY key)
SELECT DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY k.mean_streams DESC NULLS LAST) AS popularity_rank, k.key, ROUND(k.mean_streams,2) AS avg_streams, COALESCE(c.n,0) AS top50_tracks,
ROUND(100.0*COALESCE(c.n,0)/(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM top50),2) AS top50_pct,
DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COALESCE(c.n,0) DESC) AS representation_rank
FROM k LEFT JOIN c ON k.key=c.key ORDER BY popularity_rank,k.key;
note: A LEFT JOIN keeps zero-count keys. Known-key shares may total less than 100% because unknown keys are still eligible for the top 50.
steps: Calculate mean streams per known key across the full dataset. Separately select the top 50 tracks by known streams.
Count top-50 tracks by key and LEFT JOIN these counts to all known keys so zero-count keys remain.
Rank the averages and top-50 counts separately; divide counts by all 50 selected tracks, including those with unknown keys.

title: Average artist popularity >=90: Top Artist
task: Schema reasoning: check for a popularity score column. Output column_name,data_type for names containing popularity. Explain why an average >=90 cannot be interpreted as a 0–100 Spotify popularity score here. Do not rescale streams and pretend it is the missing metric.
sql:
SELECT column_name,data_type FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema='public' AND table_name='spotify' AND column_name ILIKE '%popularity%' ORDER BY column_name;
note: Not answerable from this schema. With validated per-track popularity scores and normalized credits, GROUP BY artist, HAVING AVG(popularity)>=90, and select a literal Top Artist label. Do not substitute streams>=90.
steps: Search the actual schema for a popularity field.
No such field exists, so average popularity >=90 cannot be computed as a Spotify 0–100 score.
With validated scores and individual artist credits, group by artist and filter HAVING AVG(popularity)>=90, then label qualifying rows Top Artist. Do not substitute streams>=90.
